Read with care. A flag means "have someone look", not "faulty": a station beside a road or kiln legitimately differs from its neighbours. Only 240 of the 543 stations reporting in 2025 could be checked at all, because the test compares each station with others within 25 km and many stations have none. Of those 240, 117 carry a flag, which needs just one stuck-sensor run or one sustained departure, so most flags are brief: "hours flagged" is the share of a station’s reported hours inside such an episode, and is a few percent even in the worst cities.
Stations that drifted against their neighbours
StationYears driftingLargest shift vs neighboursStatus
Punjabi Bagh, Delhi - DPCC Delhi2017more than +1,000% over 2017cleared: not drifting since
Vijay Nagar Scheme-78, Indore - Glenmark Indore2025+119% over 2025unresolved: still drifting in 2025
RVCE-Mailasandra, Bengaluru - KSPCB Bengaluru2022+42% over 2022cleared: not drifting since
Confirmed means the slope survived the multiple-testing correction and was large enough to matter. The shift is the straight-line change over that year’s days, so there is no single start date to give. Cleared means the station was audited in a later year and was not drifting; unresolved means it is still drifting in the latest year or has no later data. A station can drift because it was moved, recalibrated or re-sited, which the data cannot tell apart from a failing sensor.

Delhi, ten burning seasons

Delhi in each burning season
Delhi PM2.5, daily mean (same scale in every panel)Regional fire detections per day, Suomi NPP (same scale in every panel)
Descriptive only. These panels do not control for rain or wind, so a season with more fires and higher PM2.5 shows nothing about cause. Fire detections fall from about 100,000 a season around 2021 to under 15,000 in 2025 in this region.
Does the stubble signal repeat across seasons?
smoke exposure, p below 0.05smoke exposure, not significantwind-blind count of fires within 400 km
Under the rule fixed in advance, the replication holds. 10 of 11 seasons have a positive partial correlation (median +0.36) and 6 are significant on their own; the seasons combined give p below 0.0001. Each season uses only its rain-free days (38 to 54 of them) and controls boundary-layer height and temperature.
What this does not show. The wind-blind baseline, simply counting fires within 400 km, correlates at least as well as the wind-driven exposure in 10 of the 11 seasons, so the trajectory model adds nothing measurable over it. Only one season (2022) is significant when the test respects day-to-day autocorrelation, and with about 50 days a season that test can barely reach significance. 2015 and 2016 rest on 6 Delhi stations. The exposure index is smoke arrival, not mass: this is not a share of Delhi’s PM2.5 caused by burning.

Delhi PM2.5, fires and weather

Delhi PM2.5 and regional fire exposure
Delhi PM2.5, daily mean (left axis, µg/m³)Fire exposure index (right axis)Rain, hanging from the top (mm)
Read with care. Delhi PM2.5 stepped up the same day regional fire plumes started arriving, but the days before were rainy (about 9 mm on 26 Sep, 4 mm on 27 Sep) and 30 Sep was the first fully dry day, so rain stopping explains the step without stubble. The first look at rain-free days only, with about 10 of them, was moderate and not significant. The pre-registered test on rain-free days has not been run yet (see the counter below). Suggestive, not established, and not a share of Delhi's pollution attributable to stubble burning.
How close is the real test?
28 / 20 rain-free days with data for the stubble test
Enough dry days. By the pre-registered rule the test is run once, on 1 December.

324 stations tested in 25 regions, 4 flagged. Stations are compared only with others within about 150 km, and a region where the satellite does not track PM2.5 at all is switched off rather than flagged. The correction for multiple testing runs across the whole country.
Read with care. Satellite aerosol is a column measurement and PM2.5 a point reading at the surface; cloud and monsoon cut the number of usable days. A flag means the station follows the satellite less than its neighbours, which can be a local source as easily as a sensor fault.

Satellite AOD against Delhi PM2.5, day by day
37 days · Spearman ρ = +0.68. Few points, so treat the shape, not the number.
The satellite tracks the city's day-to-day PM2.5 but not differences between stations on the same day, so it can only check whether a station follows the same day-to-day pattern as its peers. Treat every row as a lead: a result counts only if it survives the multiple-testing correction.

How to read this page

Sub-index vs concentration. The CPCB feed reports AQI sub-indices; 100 for PM2.5 equals 60 µg/m³. Charts in µg/m³ come from OpenAQ.

Flags are leads, not verdicts. Every statistical result here is exploratory with a few weeks of data; the README lists the limits and docs/PIPELINE.md every retraction.

Nothing here is a source attribution. The stubble panels show association with fire exposure, not the share of pollution caused by it.

About

Checks whether India’s air-quality monitoring network can be trusted: data health, station drift and neighbour checks nationally, with Delhi NCR as a deeper case that adds gap filling, weather, satellite and fire evidence. It is exploratory analysis, not an official AQI or a health advisory. Source code.

Data

  • CPCB real-time AQI via data.gov.inHourly AQI sub-indices for every station in India (the live feed), plus the NCR-only file.
  • CPCB yearly station files (Vonter/india-cpcb-aqi, ODbL)15-minute station records for 2015 to 2025, republished from CPCB’s data repository.
  • OpenAQHourly PM2.5 concentrations from the same stations, in µg/m³.
  • NASA FIRMSSatellite active-fire detections and their radiative power, live and the 2015 to 2025 archive.
  • MODIS MAIAC AOD, Earth EngineAerosol optical depth, sampled at each station.
  • ERA5, Copernicus CDSWind, boundary-layer height, temperature and rain.

References

  • Benjamini and Hochberg (1995), controlling the false discovery rate
  • Lyapustin et al. (2018), MAIAC aerosol retrieval for MODIS
  • Giglio et al. (2016), MODIS Collection 6 active fire detection
  • Hersbach et al. (2020), the ERA5 reanalysis (dataset page)
  • Air quality index categories (India section)
